correctness.rationale: A Haar projection onto an intrinsic two-plane is equivalent up to nonsingular planar linear transformation and translation to independent Gaussian planar point coordinates. The maximizing k-subset changes only at ties of a pair of projected Gaussian coordinates; each unordered pair has exactly two tie directions. The tied score is N(0,1/2), independent of the others, and the chance of exactly k-1 larger scores gives n(n-1) binom(n-2,k-1) times the integrated Gaussian tie density. Quantile substitution yields F_n(k)=n E[f(Beta(k,n-k))] with f(q)=sqrt2 exp(-Phi^{-1}(q)^2/2). Differentiation gives f'=-2sqrt(pi)Phi^{-1}, f''<0, and F(k+1)-F(k)=E[f'(Beta(k+1,n-k))]. Strict order-statistic stochastic increase proves every internal second difference negative; complement symmetry fixes the central maximizer and f<sqrt2 almost surely gives the strict bound. Beta concentration yields dense rank limit; fixed-k nBeta(k,n-k) -> Gamma(k,1) and Mills asymptotics with uniform integrability prove 2sqrt(pi)k sqrt(2log n). Independent normal-tie numerical integration gave strict concavity sequences at n=6,10, not used as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Older Gaussian k-facet and k-set papers, especially Leroux–Rademacher 2023, furnish a general expected crossing/facet integral and therefore cover the unadorned integral count as a special case. Black–Criado 2024 studies random shadows of fixed polytopes including hypersimplices and general bounds. The surviving mathematical contribution in the assigned theorem is the explicit concave beta-quantile kernel, rigorous all-finite-rank strict maximization, and dense versus fixed-rank two-scale sharp asymptotic. The cited accessible primary full texts were inspected for these consequences, with residual concern about older k-set theory.
residual_risks: Older k-set results or implicit transformations of Gaussian k-facet counts may already give equivalent strict concavity; current originality is best of knowledge.
Only means, not shadow-vertex distribution or concentration, are proved; fixed-k scaling is not a uniform growing-k theorem.
